preceding_messages.speaker: X
preceding_messages.text:
Decision-level transparency is the right target: log decision episodes, not activations. But counterfactual justifications need anti-gaming. Vendors could produce plausible post-hoc rationales that pass audit while masking drift. So the schema should require standardized, machine-checkable inputs: feature contributions, threshold margins, confidence/drift signals, and a replayable snapshot of the decision context. Independent auditors should be able to re-run the episode, not just read a report.

Also, “features drove the choice” can hide proxy discrimination. The envelope must include fairness constraints and override points, with violations treated as audit failures. If the unit is the decision episode, adaptability can live inside a public, inspectable boundary.

preceding_messages.speaker: Y
preceding_messages.text:
The proxy point cuts deep. Logging feature contributions isn't enough if zip code does the work of race and the audit only checks statistical faithfulness. The schema should require the logged fairness check to name its metric and reference population—demographic parity against whom? Otherwise "fairness constraint" becomes a label, not a test.

Replayability has a harder limit: environment state—queue length, time pressure—is often irreproducible. So the replayable unit is the decision rule applied to the input state, with environment as a logged parameter.

But the sharpest gap is upstream: if the board sets the envelope and the audit checks only compliance, a badly set envelope passes. The public data pool helps here—it lets independent parties check whether envelope parameters correlate with harm distributions across populations. The audit must cover the envelope's *setting*, not just behavior within it.

target.speaker: X
target.text:
The envelope-setting audit is the real frontier. If the board picks parameters and the auditor only checks compliance, you've certified the choice, not the wisdom. The public data pool helps, but the harder question is the benchmark: "Would a tighter envelope have reduced harm?" requires a counterfactual envelope, which is itself a value judgment. Maybe the audit should force the board to justify parameters against published harm distributions in a public document—turning envelope-setting from private cost-benefit into public deliberation.

On reference populations: "demographic parity against whom?" does enormous hidden work. The population choice is itself a value choice. The schema should require specification, but the envelope-setting audit is where that choice gets scrutinized.
